write.ko: 예를 들어, 그녀는 바닥이 평평한 종이봉투를 만드는 기계를 발명하였는데, 이것은 사람들이 식료품을 더 쉽게 운반하고 점심 도시 락을 더 쉽게 가지고 다닐 수 있도록 했다.
write.en: For example, she invented a machine for producing flat- bottomed paper bags, which enabled people to carry groceries and pack lunches more easily.

write.ko: 1989년 그는 월드 와이드 웹이라고 불리는 정보 시스템을 개발했는데, 이는 현재 우리가 매일 사용하는 것이다.
write.en: In 1989, he invented an information system called the World Wide Web, which we now use on a daily basis.

write.ko: 하지만 Berners-Lee는 그의 발명품으로 엄청난 돈을 벌 수 있었음에도 불구하고 그것을 대중에게 무료로 배포하기로 결정했다.
write.en: However, Berners-Lee decided to distribute his invention to the public for free, even though he could have made a fortune from it.

write.ko: 프랑스의 교육자 Louis Braille는 자신의 발명품인 Braille 시스템으로 시각 장애인들의 삶에 큰 변화를 가져왔다. 204
write.en: Louis Braille, a French educator, brought a significant change to the lives of blind people through his invention of the Braille system.

write.ko: Braille의 발명품은 시각 장애인들이 문자로 된 정보에 접근하고 독립적으로 의사소통할 수 있게 했다.
write.en: Braille's invention has empowered blind people to access written information and communicate independently.

write.ko: 그것은 오늘날에도 시각 장애인들에게 계속 혜택을 주고, 지속적인 영향을 미치고 있다.
write.en: It continues to benefit the blind community today, leaving a lasting impact.

write.ko: Marie Curie는 방사능에 대한 선구적인 연구로 널리 인정받지만, 그녀가 제1차 세계 대전 중에 의료 분야에서도 중요한 역할을 했 다는 것을 아는 사람은 거의 없을 것이다.
write.en: While Marie Curie is widely recognized for her pioneering work on radioactivity, few may know that she also played a significant role in the medical field during World War I.

write.ko: Curie의 혁신적인 해결책은 엑스선 기기가 장착되어 있고 특수 훈련을 받은 엑스선 조작자가 배치된 차량을 만드는 것이었다. 205
write.en: Curie's innovative solution was to create a vehicle equipped with an X-ray machine and staffed with a specially trained X- ray operator.

write.ko: 'Little Curies'라고도 알려진 이 이동 차량은 전투 현장으로 바로 운전되어 의사들이 부상병들의 몸속에서 부러진 뼈를 확인하고 작은 금속 조각들을 찾을 수 있도록 했다.
write.en: These mobile units, also known as "Little Curies," were driven directly to the battle sites, allowing doctors to see broken bones and find small pieces of metal in the bodies of wounded soldiers.

read.ko: 1932년 11월 말 어느 날 저녁, 몹시 차가운 바람이 거세게 부는 가운데 두 명의 인물이 실험실에서 모습을 드러낸다.
read.en: One evening in late November 1932, a bitterly cold wind blows fiercely as two figures emerge from a laboratory.

read.ko: 그들이 파산한 은행들, 붕괴된 산업, 그리고 널리 퍼진 절망의 세계 — 3년간의 대공황으로 폐허가 된 세계 — 로 나아갈 때 어둠이 내리기 시작한다.
read.en: Darkness begins to fall as they set out into a world of failed banks, collapsed industry, and widespread despair — a world ruined by three years of the Great Depression.

read.ko: 근무는 끝났지만, Pearl Kendrick과 Grace Eldering에게는 다른 종류의 일이 시작될 참이다.
read.en: The workday has come to an end, but for Pearl Kendrick and Grace Eldering, a different kind of work is about to begin.

read.ko: 그들은 백일해라고 불리는 치명적인 질병으로 고통받고 있는 어린이들의 집들을 방문하러 가는 길이다.
read.en: They are on their way to visit the homes of children suffering from a deadly disease called pertussis.

read.ko: 두 여성은 집집마다 돌아다니면서 희미한 램프 불빛에 의지해 아픈 아이들의 검체를 수집한다.
read.en: The two women go from home to home collecting samples from the sick children by the faint light of their lamps.

read.ko: 걷잡을 수 없이 기침하며 숨을 쉬기 위해 고군분투하는 아이들이 간신히 생을 붙잡고 있을 때, 그들은 자포자기하고 실직한 부모들의 비극적인 이야기를 듣는다.
read.en: They listen to the tragic stories of desperate and unemployed parents as the children, coughing uncontrollably and struggling to breathe, barely hold on to life.

read.ko: 백일해는 심각한 기침, 호흡 곤란, 그리고 이 질병에 걸린 사람들이 숨을 들이쉬려 할 때 내는 고음의 '흡(whooping)' 소리로 특징 지어지는 세균성 질환이다.
read.en: Pertussis is a bacterial disease characterized by serious coughing, breathing difficulties, and the high-pitched "whooping" sound that people with the disease make as they try to breathe in.

read.ko: 이 독특한 소리 때문에 사람들은 이 질병을 'whooping cough(백일해)'라고 부르기 시작했다. 197
read.en: Because of this distinct sound, people started to call the disease "whooping cough."

read.ko: 오랫동안, 이 끔찍한 병은 어린아이들이 있는 가정의 가장 큰 공포 중 하나였는데, 백일해에 걸린 아기는 사망할 확률이 높았기 때문 이다.
read.en: For a long time, this terrible illness was one of the greatest terrors of families with young children, because babies who contracted it had a high chance of dying.

read.ko: 1930년대에, 미국에서는 매년 평균 6,000명이 백일해로 사망했다.
read.en: In the 1930s, an average of 6,000 people died of whooping cough in the United States each year.

read.ko: 그들 중 95%가 5세 미만의 어린이였다.
read.en: Ninety-five percent of them were children under five years of age.

read.ko: 그 질병의 원인은 1906년에 밝혀졌지만, 개발된 백신은 효과가 없었다.
read.en: The cause of the disease had been identified in 1906, but the vaccines that had been developed were ineffective.

read.ko: 과학자들과 연구원들은 효과적인 백신을 만들기 위해 20년 이상 노력했지만, 그들의 노력은 성과가 없었다 — Kendrick과 Eldering이 나타나기 전까지는 말이다.
read.en: Scientists and researchers worked for more than 20 years to produce an effective one, but their efforts were fruitless — until Kendrick and Eldering came along.

read.ko: Pearl Kendrick은 대학에서 세균학을 공부했고 1920년 미시간주 보건부에 채용되었다.
read.en: Pearl Kendrick studied bacteriology in university and was recruited by the Michigan Department of Health in 1920.

read.ko: 그녀가 동료 세균학자인 Grace Eldering을 만난 것은 바로 그곳에서였다.
read.en: It was there that she met fellow bacteriologist Grace Eldering.

read.ko: 두 사람은 빠르게 유대감을 형성했고, 1932년에 백일해 백신을 함께 연구하기 시작했다.
read.en: The two quickly bonded, and in 1932 they started working together on a vaccine for whooping cough.

read.ko: 개인적 경험이 두 사람 모두에게 (연구에 대한) 동기가 되었는데, 둘 다 어린 시절 백일해를 직접 이겨냈고 그 질병의 극심한 고통을 기억하고 있었기 때문이다. 198
read.en: Personal experience served as motivation for both of them, as they had each survived whooping cough as children themselves and remembered the severe pain of the disease.

read.ko: 두 과학자는 또한 아이들의 건강을 증진시키기를 간절히 바랐다.
read.en: Both scientists were also eager to promote children's health.

read.ko: 안타깝게도 대공황으로 인해 연구 자금이 극히 제한되었다.
read.en: Unfortunately, research funding was extremely limited due to the Great Depression.

read.ko: 또한 Kendrick과 Eldering은 부가적인 프로젝트로 백신을 개발해야 했다.
read.en: Also, Kendrick and Eldering had to develop the vaccine as a side project.

read.ko: 그것은 마치 어떠한 보수도 받지 못하는 두 번째 직업을 갖는 것과 같았다.
read.en: It was like having a second job for which they never received any payment.

read.ko: 그럼에도 불구하고 그들은 매일 일상적인 업무를 마치고 나면, 그들이 열의를 가진 일을 시작하곤 했다.
read.en: Still, when they finished their normal duties each day, they would get started on the work that they were enthusiastic about.

read.ko: 그들이 직면한 어려움들은 그들이 목표를 향해 끈질기게 나아가는 것을 막지 못했다.
read.en: The difficulties they faced did not stop them from persisting toward their goal.

read.ko: 그들은 돈을 추가로 벌기 위해 그 일을 한 것이 아니었다. 그보다는, 그들은 죄 없는 아이들과 그들의 가족들의 고통을 덜어주기 위 해 연구했다.
read.en: They did not do the work to make extra money; instead, they worked to relieve the suffering of innocent children and their families.

read.ko: 그들은 백일해의 원인이 되는 세균의 검체를 수집함으로써 백신을 개발하는 과정을 시작했다.
read.en: They began the process of developing their vaccine by gathering samples of the bacteria that cause whooping cough.

read.ko: 그들을 지원하기 위해, 지역 의사들과 간호사들은 그들의 환자들에게서 얻은 '기침판'을 제공했다. 199
read.en: To support them, local doctors and nurses provided "cough plates" from their patients.

read.ko: 환자들은 페트리 접시 위에 기침했고, 그런 다음 그것은 세균 배양기에 넣어졌다.
read.en: The patients coughed onto a petri dish, which was then put into an incubator.

read.ko: 이는 세균이 Kendrick과 Eldering이 분석할 수 있는 군집으로 자라게 했다.
read.en: This allowed the bacteria to grow into colonies that Kendrick and Eldering could analyze.

read.ko: 직접 검체를 수집할 때, 그들은 아픈 아이들의 집으로 가곤 했다.
read.en: When they collected samples on their own, they would go to the homes of sick children.

read.ko: 그때마다, 그들은 그 병에 의해 야기된 끔찍한 고통을 다시 한번 떠올렸다.
read.en: Each time, they were reminded once again of the dreadful suffering caused by the disease.

read.ko: 이 무고한 어린 희생자들이 기침하고 숨쉬기 위해 고군분투하는 모습은 효과적인 백신의 시급한 필요성을 강력하게 상기시켰다.
read.en: The sight of these innocent young victims coughing and struggling to breathe was a powerful reminder of the urgent need for an effective vaccine.

read.ko: Kendrick과 Eldering은 세균을 연구하며 많은 긴 밤을 보냈고, 마침내 잠재적인 백신을 생산해 냈다.
read.en: Kendrick and Eldering spent many long nights studying the bacteria and finally produced a potential vaccine.

read.ko: 그러나 임상 실험을 실시하기 전에, 그들은 그것이 실험 대상자들에게 어떠한 부정적인 부작용도 일으키지 않을 것이라는 것을 확실 히 해야 했다.
read.en: Before they performed any clinical trials, though, they had to be certain that it would not have any negative side effects on the subjects.

read.ko: 그들은 많은 실험실 시험을 실행했고, 심지어 그들은 그것이 안전하다는 것을 확인하기 위해 스스로에게 주사했다.
read.en: They ran many laboratory tests, and they even injected it into themselves to confirm that it was safe.

read.ko: 1934년부터 1935년까지, 그들은 1,592명의 아이들을 대상으로 첫 현장 실험을 실시했다. 200
read.en: From 1934 to 1935, they conducted their first field test with 1,592 children.

read.ko: 백신을 접종한 712명의 아이들의 그룹에서, 단지 4명만이 백일해에 걸렸고, 이 사례들 중 어떠한 사례도 심각하지 않았다.
read.en: In the group of 712 vaccinated children, only four developed whooping cough, and none of these cases were serious.

read.ko: 백신의 분명한 성공에도 불구하고, Kendrick과 Eldering은 백신의 효과에 대한 추가 확인을 원했다.
read.en: Despite the apparent success of the vaccine, Kendrick and Eldering wanted further confirmation of its effectiveness.

read.ko: 그들은 연구를 확대하고 더 큰 그룹의 어린이들을 대상으로 더 많은 실험을 진행하기로 굳게 결심했다.
read.en: They became determined to expand their research and run more tests with larger groups of children.

read.ko: 그러나 그들은 심각한 자금 부족에 직면하고 있었기 때문에 (연구와 실험을) 계속 진행할 수 없었다.
read.en: However, they were unable to proceed because they were facing a severe lack of funds.

read.ko: 수천 명의 어린이들이 계속해서 그 질병으로 고통받고 있는 가운데, 그들은 절망적인 상황에 처했다.
read.en: With thousands of children continuing to suffer from the disease, they found themselves in a desperate situation.

read.ko: 다행히도 그들은 예상치 못한 인물로부터 도움을 받았다.
read.en: Luckily, they got help from an unexpected figure.

read.ko: 1936년에 영부인 Eleanor Roosevelt가 직접 실험실을 방문했고 Kendrick과 Eldering이 백일해와의 싸움에 기울이는 노력을 직 접 보았다.
read.en: In 1936, First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt herself visited the laboratory and saw with her own eyes the efforts that Kendrick and Eldering were making in their battle against whooping cough.

read.ko: 남편이 소아마비를 앓았던 Eleanor Roosevelt는 전염병을 퇴치하는 것에 관심이 많았다.
read.en: Eleanor Roosevelt, whose husband suffered from polio, was interested in fighting infectious diseases.

read.ko: 그녀는 두 여성과 함께 시간을 보냈고, 그들의 일의 엄청난 중요성을 깨닫게 되었다. 201
read.en: She spent time with the women and came to realize the enormous importance of their work.

read.ko: 그녀의 도움으로 Kendrick과 Eldering은 대규모 실험을 실시하기에 충분한 자금을 확보할 수 있었다.
read.en: With her help, Kendrick and Eldering were able to secure enough funding to conduct a large-scale trial.

read.ko: 1937년까지 Kendrick과 Eldering은 4,200명 이상의 어린이들을 그들의 실험에 포함시킬 수 있었다.
read.en: By 1937, Kendrick and Eldering were able to include more than 4,200 children in their trial.

read.ko: 첫 번째 현장 실험에서와 같이, 백신을 접종한 그룹은 질병에 대해 높은 수준의 면역력을 보여주었다.
read.en: Just as in their first field test, the vaccinated group demonstrated a high level of immunity against the disease.

read.ko: 과학계는 그 결과에 깜짝 놀랐고, 1940년에 백신이 미국 전역으로 배포되기 시작했다.
read.en: The scientific community was amazed at the results, and, in 1940, the vaccine started being distributed all across the United States.

read.ko: 4년 후, 이것은 미국 의학 협회의 권장 예방접종 목록에 추가되었고, 얼마 지나지 않아 백일해 감염은 극적으로 감소했다.
read.en: Four years later, it was added to the American Medical Association's list of recommended immunizations, and soon after, there was a dramatic decline in whooping cough infections.

read.ko: 1934년에 7,518명에 달했던 백일해로 인한 연간 사망자 수는 1970년대 중반에 10명 미만으로 떨어졌다.
read.en: In the mid-1970s, the number of annual deaths caused by whooping cough, which had reached 7,518 in 1934, dropped to under 10.

read.ko: Kendrick과 Eldering은 그들이 백신으로 특허를 받았더라면 매우 부유해질 수도 있었을 것이라는 말을 자주 들었다.
read.en: Kendrick and Eldering were often told that they could have become very wealthy if they had patented their vaccine.

read.ko: 그러나 그들은 그것은 둘이서만 만든 것이 아니라, 다른 많은 사람들의 도움으로 만들어졌다고 대답했다.
read.en: However, they replied that it had not been created by them alone, but with the help of many others.

read.ko: 그들은 또한 자신들의 큰 공헌을 드러내고 싶지 않아 개인적인 인터뷰를 피했다. 202
read.en: They also avoided personal interviews, not wanting to reveal the great contribution they had made.

read.ko: 그들은 진정으로 백신을 만드는 도전을 즐겼기 때문에, 그들이 받는 지나친 칭찬은 그들을 불편하게 만든다고 말했다.
read.en: They said that they had genuinely enjoyed the challenge of creating the vaccine, so the excessive praise that they received made them uncomfortable.

read.ko: 결국, 그들의 노고 덕분에 매우 많은 생명이 구해지고 있다는 것을 아는 것만으로도 이 놀랍고도 겸손한 영웅들에게는 충분한 보상 인 것이었다.
read.en: In the end, knowing that so many lives were being saved thanks to their hard work was enough of a reward for these remarkable and modest heroes.

read.ko: 사람들을 돕고 세상을 더 나은 곳으로 만들기 위해 자신의 기발한 아이디어를 사용했던 특별한 사람들이 있다.
read.en: There are some special individuals who used their brilliant ideas to help people and make the world a better place.

read.ko: 그들은 누구이며 사회에 어떻게 기여했는지 알아보자.
read.en: Get ready to learn who they are and how they contributed to society.

read.ko: 1838년에 태어난 Margaret E. Knight는 목공 공구로 무언가를 만드는 것을 좋아하던 발명가였다.
read.en: Born in 1838, Margaret E. Knight was an inventor who loved making things with her wood-working tools.

read.ko: 어느 날 Margaret은 공장에서 끔찍한 사고를 목격했다.
read.en: One day, Margaret witnessed a terrible accident at a factory.

read.ko: 베틀의 한 조각이 부러져 공중으로 날아가 어린 노동자를 다치게 했다.
read.en: A piece of a loom broke off, flew through the air, and hurt a young worker.

read.ko: 이 일이 다시 일어나는 것을 막기 위해 Margaret은 기계가 제대로 작동하지 않을 경우 그것을 즉시 멈추게 하는 장치를 발명했다.
read.en: To prevent this from happening again, Margaret invented a device that would immediately stop the machine if it failed to function properly.

para.en: One evening in late November 1932, a bitterly cold wind blows fiercely as two figures emerge from a laboratory. Darkness begins to fall as they set out into a world of failed banks, collapsed industry, and widespread despair — a world ruined by three years of the Great Depression. The workday has come to an end, but for Pearl Kendrick and Grace Eldering, a different kind of work is about to begin. They are on their way to visit the homes of children suffering from a deadly disease called pertussis. The two women go from home to home collecting samples from the sick children by the faint light of their lamps. They listen to the tragic stories of desperate and unemployed parents as the children, coughing uncontrollably and struggling to breathe, barely barely on to life.

Pertussis is a bacterial disease characterized by serious coughing, breathing difficulties, and the high-pitched "whooping" sound that people with the disease make as they try to breathe in. Because of this distinct sound, people started to call the disease "whooping cough." For a long time, this terrible illness was one of the greatest terrors of families with young children, because babies who contracted it had a high chance of dying. In the 1930s, an average of 6,000 people died of whooping cough in the United States each year. Ninety-five percent of them were children under five years of age. The cause of the disease had been identified in 1906, but the vaccines that had been developed were ineffective. Scientists and researchers worked for more than 20 years to produce an effective one, but their efforts were fruitless — until Kendrick and Eldering came along.

Pearl Kendrick studied bacteriology in university and was recruited by the Michigan Department of Health in 1920. It was there that she met fellow bacteriologist Grace Eldering. The two quickly bonded, and in 1932 they started working together on a vaccine for whooping cough. Personal experience served as motivation for both of them, as they had each survived whooping cough as children themselves and remembered the severe pain of the disease. Both scientists were also eager to promote children's health. Unfortunately, research funding was extremely limited due to the Great Depression. Also, Kendrick and Eldering had to develop the vaccine as a side project. It was like having a second job for which they never received any payment. Still, when they finished their normal duties each day, they would get started on the work that they were enthusiastic about. The difficulties they faced did not stop them from persisting toward their goal. They did not do the work to make extra money; instead, they worked to relieve the suffering of innocent children and their families. 115 2

They began the process of developing their vaccine by gathering samples of the bacteria that cause whooping cough. To support them local doctors and nurses provided "cough plates" from their patients. The patients coughed onto a petri dish which was then put into an incubator. This allowed the bacteria to grow into colonies that Kendrick and Eldering could analyze. When they collected samples on their own they would go to the homes of sick children. Each time they were reminded once again of the dreadful suffering caused by the disease. The sight of these innocent young victims coughing and struggling to breathe was a powerful reminder of the urgent need for an effective vaccine. Kendrick and Eldering spent many long nights studying the bacteria and finally produced a potential vaccine. Before they performed any clinical trials though they had to be certain that it would not have any negative side effects on the subjects. They ran many laboratory tests and they even injected it into themselves to confirm that it was safe. From 1934 to 1935 they conducted their first field test with 1,592 children. In the group of 712 vaccinated children only four developed whooping cough and none of these cases were serious.

Despite the apparent success of the vaccine, Kendrick and Eldering wanted further confirmation of its effectiveness They became determined to expand their research and run more tests with larger groups of children. However, they were unable to proceed because they were facing a severe lack of funds. With thousands of children continuing to suffer from the disease, they found themselves in a desperate situation. Luckily, they got help from an unexpected figure. In 1936, First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt herself visited the laboratory and saw with her own eyes the efforts that Kendrick and Eldering were making in their battle against whooping cough. Eleanor Roosevelt, whose husband suffered from polio, was interested in fighting infectious diseases. She spent time with the women and came to realize the enormous importance of their work. With her help, Kendrick and Eldering were able to secure enough funding to conduct a large-scale trial.

trial By 1937, Kendrick and Eldering were able to include more than 4,200 children in their trial. Just as in their first field test, the vaccinated group demonstrated a high level of immunity against the disease. The scientific community was amazed at the results, and, in 1940, the vaccine started being distributed all across the United States. Four years later, it was added to the American Medical Association's list of recommended immunizations, and soon after, there was a dramatic decline in whooping cough infections. In the mid-1970s, the number of annual deaths caused by whooping cough, which had reached 7,518 in 1934, dropped to under 10. 116 3

Kendrick and Eldering were often told that they could have become very wealthy if they had patented their vaccine. However, they replied that it had not been created by them alone, but with the help of many others. They also avoided personal interviews, not wanting to reveal the great contribution they had made. They said that they had genuinely enjoyed the challenge of creating the vaccine, so the excessive praise that they received made them uncomfortable. In the end, knowing that so many lives were being saved thanks to their hard work was enough of a reward for these remarkable and modest heroes.

There are some special individuals who used their brilliant ideas to help people and make the world a better place. Get ready to learn who they are and how they contributed to society. Born in 1838, Margaret E. Knight was an inventor who loved making things with her wood-working tools. One day, Margaret witnessed a terrible accident at a factory. A piece of a loom broke off, flew through the air, and hurt a young worker. To prevent this from happening again, Margaret invented a device that would immediately stop the machine if it failed to function properly. Soon her invention was adopted by factories across the country. Knight also created other inventions that improved people's lives. For example, she invented a machine for producing flat-bottomed paper bags, which enabled people to carry groceries and pack lunches more easily.

Tim Berners-Lee is a British computer scientist. In 1989, he invented an information system called the World Wide Web, which we now use on a daily basis. It revolutionized the way we access the Internet, and it has had a profound social and economic impact. The original idea behind the World Wide Web was to make it easier for scientists from different universities to share information and communicate with one another. However, Berners-Lee decided to distribute his invention to the public for free, even though he could have made a fortune from it. This is because he strongly believed that the technology like the Internet should belong to everyone, not just a few companies. 117 4

Louis Braille, a French educator, brought a significant change to the lives of blind people through his invention of the Braille system. This reading and writing system uses different combinations of six dots to represent each letter in a word. It was inspired by a note-taking system of embossed dots used by the army. Braille also excelled in music, and he expanded the Braille system to music and mathematics. The Braille system has been adapted to more than 100 languages and is used all over the world. Braille's invention has empowered blind people to access written information and communicate independently. It continues to benefit the blind community today, leaving a lasting impact.

While Marie Curie is widely recognized for her pioneering work on radioactivity, few may know that she also played a significant role in the medical field during World War I. At that time, X-ray machines were available only in city hospitals, far from the battle sites where injured soldiers were being treated. Curie's innovative solution was to create a vehicle equipped with an X-ray machine and staffed with a specially trained X-ray operator. These mobile units, also known as "Little Curies," were driven directly to the battle sites, allowing doctors to see broken bones and find small pieces of metal in the bodies of wounded soldiers. Marie Curie herself drove one to help save lives!
